title: Sparse representations and dropout
summary: Sparse parameters, sparse representations, and dropout masks create zeros in different objects. Their objectives, effects during training, and behavior at inference are distinct.
search: Three meanings of “sparse” A parameter vector is sparse when many learned coefficients are zero. A representation is sparse when an example uses only a few latent features. A dropout mask creates temporary zeros in a computation. Similar-looking zeros do not make the mechanisms equivalent. For sparse coding, write x\approx Da , where D is a dictionary and a is the code. The code solves \hat a\in\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_a\left[\frac12\lVert x-Da\rVert^2+\lambda\lVert a\rVert_1\right]. The dictionary can have more columns than input dimensions; each example still uses only a small subset. This is representation sparsity , not necessarily a sparse dictionary or a sparse network parameter matrix. Rarely active hidden units A sparse autoencoder can penalize average hidden activity. If \hat\rho_j is unit j ’s observed mean activity and \rho is the desired small activity, one penalty is \sum_j\operatorname{KL}(\rho\Vert\hat\rho_j), where the Bernoulli divergence is \operatorname{KL}(\rho\Vert\hat\rho)=\rho\log\frac\rho{\hat\rho}+(1-\rho)\log\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat\rho}. This expression assumes the activity quantities have the probability-like interpretation required by the Bernoulli divergence. It should not be applied mechanically to unrestricted hidden values. The aim is for units to be useful selectively across examples. Step by step Differentiate the sparse-activation KL penalty all the way to one activation Setting. A hidden unit has activations a_1,\ldots,a_B\in(0,1) and empirical mean \hat\rho=B^{-1}\sum_i a_i . A target activity \rho\in(0,1) is fixed. Bernoulli KL requires both probabilities to lie strictly between zero and one for this finite formula. 1 · Write the two possible Bernoulli outcomes For outcome one the probabilities are \rho and \hat\rho ; for outcome zero they are 1-\rho and 1-\hat\rho . By the definition of discrete KL, K(\hat\rho)=\rho\log\frac\rho{\hat\rho}+(1-\rho)\log\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat\rho}. 2 · Separate constant and variable logarithms K=\rho\log\rho-\rho\log\hat\rho+(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho)-(1-\rho)\log(1-\hat\rho). Differentiate with respect to \hat\rho : K'(\hat\rho)=-\frac\rho{\hat\rho}+\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat\rho} =\frac{\hat\rho-\rho}{\hat\rho(1-\hat\rho)}. The denominator is positive, so the derivative points toward the target mean. 3 · Verify the minimum The derivative is zero at \hat\rho=\rho , and K''(\hat\rho)=\frac\rho{\hat\rho^2}+\frac{1-\rho}{(1-\hat\rho)^2}>0. Thus this is the unique minimum, with KL equal to zero. 4 · Continue through averaging and an activation Since \partial\hat\rho/\partial a_i=1/B , \frac{\partial K}{\partial a_i}=\frac1B\left[-\frac\rho{\hat\rho}+\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat\rho}\right]. If a_i=\sigma(z_i) , multiply by a_i(1-a_i) to obtain \partial K/\partial z_i . A total objective weighted by \gamma multiplies this contribution by \gamma . Every example contributes to the shared mean, so this regularizer couples observations in a batch. 5 · Do not apply the probability formula blindly An unconstrained ReLU activation can exceed one, so its average is not automatically a Bernoulli probability. Use a compatible bounded activation/statistic or a different sparsity penalty. Clamping for numerical safety changes gradients at the clamped boundary and should be explicit. Dropout’s stochastic mechanism Let h be a hidden activation vector and q=1-p the keep probability, with 0<q\le1 for the scaling formula below. In inverted dropout, m_j\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q),\qquad\tilde h=\frac{m\odot h}{q}. Conditioning on the original activation, \mathbb E[\tilde h_j\mid h_j]=h_j . Scaling during training therefore preserves the activation’s expectation, and the full activation is used without that random mask during ordinary evaluation. For example, take h=(2,1,-3,4) , p=0.5 , and mask (1,0,1,0) . The result is (4,0,-6,0) . Dropping half the entries does not mean the surviving entries retain their original value under inverted scaling. Outputs from random dropout masks and a deterministic evaluation pass. Preserving an activation’s expectation does not make the output of a nonlinear network equal to the average output of all its masked versions. Regularization · PDF p. 20 Step by step Derive dropout’s mean, variance, and a nonlinear counterexample Setting. Treat an activation h as fixed and draw m\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q) , with keep probability 0<q\le1 . Inverted dropout returns \tilde h=mh/q . The case q=0 is excluded from this analytic scaling formula. 1 · Evaluate the two possible values With probability q , \tilde h=h/q . With probability 1-q , \tilde h=0 . Hence \mathbb E[\tilde h]=q\frac hq+(1-q)0=h. 2 · Calculate the second moment, then the variance \mathbb E[\tilde h^2]=q\frac{h^2}{q^2}=\frac{h^2}{q}, \operatorname{Var}(\tilde h)=\mathbb E[\tilde h^2]-\mathbb E[\tilde h]^2 =\frac{1-q}{q}h^2. At q=1/2 , the two values are 0 and 2h , with mean h and variance h^2 . 3 · Pass the noise through a linear output For independent masks m_j and s=\sum_jw_jm_jh_j/q , linearity gives \mathbb E[s]=\sum_jw_jh_j . Independence makes cross covariances zero, so \operatorname{Var}(s)=\frac{1-q}{q}\sum_jw_j^2h_j^2. For squared loss and fixed target y , \mathbb E[(s-y)^2]=(\mathbb E[s]-y)^2+\operatorname{Var}(s). In this particular linear-output case, dropout adds a feature-dependent quadratic penalty. It is not a universal single L2 coefficient for an entire nonlinear network. 4 · Show why the full deterministic network need not equal the stochastic mean Take h=1 , q=1/2 , and a following transformation f(u)=\operatorname{ReLU}(u-1) . The stochastic outputs are f(0)=0 and f(2)=1 , so \mathbb E[f(\tilde h)]=1/2 . But f(\mathbb E[\tilde h])=f(1)=0 . Preserving a layer’s activation mean does not allow expectation to pass through every later nonlinearity. 5 · Connect the identity to evaluation behavior Ordinary inverted-dropout evaluation uses the unchanged activation h instead of resampling and does not multiply it by q again. This matches the layerwise scaling convention, not an exact integration over all possible nonlinear subnetworks. Why it can regularize Dropout discourages co-adaptation by preventing a unit from relying on the same partners in every training pass. It also trains many parameter-sharing subnetworks and adds multiplicative noise to their internal features. These are complementary ways to interpret its regularizing effect. The expectation identity is local to the masked activation. A nonlinear downstream function generally does not commute with expectation. Treating dropout as a related-subnetwork ensemble is therefore an intuition, not an exact statement that one deterministic pass equals all-network averaging. Dropout does not erase learned weights After a masked training pass, the weights still exist. In ordinary evaluation the network uses all units. LASSO’s exact parameter zeros and a sparse code’s selective activation pattern are different from these temporary masks. The probability p is a hyperparameter, not a desired fraction of permanently removed parameters. Excessive dropout can create underfitting and noisy optimization. Placement depends on architecture: convolutional, recurrent, residual, and Transformer components have different conventions. Read train and evaluation behavior explicitly Module evaluation mode disables ordinary dropout masks. Disabling autograd only changes graph recording; it does not switch dropout to evaluation behavior. The two controls serve different purposes. Use the model’s intended training/evaluation modes during metric calculation. derivations.title: Differentiate the sparse-activation KL penalty all the way to one activation
derivations.search: Setting. A hidden unit has activations a_1,\ldots,a_B\in(0,1) and empirical mean \hat\rho=B^{-1}\sum_i a_i . A target activity \rho\in(0,1) is fixed. Bernoulli KL requires both probabilities to lie strictly between zero and one for this finite formula. 1 · Write the two possible Bernoulli outcomes For outcome one the probabilities are \rho and \hat\rho ; for outcome zero they are 1-\rho and 1-\hat\rho . By the definition of discrete KL, K(\hat\rho)=\rho\log\frac\rho{\hat\rho}+(1-\rho)\log\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat\rho}. 2 · Separate constant and variable logarithms K=\rho\log\rho-\rho\log\hat\rho+(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho)-(1-\rho)\log(1-\hat\rho). Differentiate with respect to \hat\rho : K'(\hat\rho)=-\frac\rho{\hat\rho}+\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat\rho} =\frac{\hat\rho-\rho}{\hat\rho(1-\hat\rho)}. The denominator is positive, so the derivative points toward the target mean. 3 · Verify the minimum The derivative is zero at \hat\rho=\rho , and K''(\hat\rho)=\frac\rho{\hat\rho^2}+\frac{1-\rho}{(1-\hat\rho)^2}>0. Thus this is the unique minimum, with KL equal to zero. 4 · Continue through averaging and an activation Since \partial\hat\rho/\partial a_i=1/B , \frac{\partial K}{\partial a_i}=\frac1B\left[-\frac\rho{\hat\rho}+\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat\rho}\right]. If a_i=\sigma(z_i) , multiply by a_i(1-a_i) to obtain \partial K/\partial z_i . A total objective weighted by \gamma multiplies this contribution by \gamma . Every example contributes to the shared mean, so this regularizer couples observations in a batch. 5 · Do not apply the probability formula blindly An unconstrained ReLU activation can exceed one, so its average is not automatically a Bernoulli probability. The case q=0 is excluded from this analytic scaling formula. 1 · Evaluate the two possible values With probability q , \tilde h=h/q . With probability 1-q , \tilde h=0 . Hence \mathbb E[\tilde h]=q\frac hq+(1-q)0=h. 2 · Calculate the second moment, then the variance \mathbb E[\tilde h^2]=q\frac{h^2}{q^2}=\frac{h^2}{q}, \operatorname{Var}(\tilde h)=\mathbb E[\tilde h^2]-\mathbb E[\tilde h]^2 =\frac{1-q}{q}h^2. At q=1/2 , the two values are 0 and 2h , with mean h and variance h^2 . 3 · Pass the noise through a linear output For independent masks m_j and s=\sum_jw_jm_jh_j/q , linearity gives \mathbb E[s]=\sum_jw_jh_j . title: Bagging, random forests, and out-of-bag evaluation
summary: Bagging fits models to bootstrap samples and combines their predictions. The variance reduction depends on both the variability of individual models and the correlation between them.
search: Bootstrap aggregating Bagging trains models on perturbed versions of the dataset and combines their predictions. An ordinary bootstrap draws n observations with replacement from n originals. Some rows appear repeatedly; others are absent. The probability that a particular row is omitted is \left(1-\frac1n\right)^n\longrightarrow e^{-1}\approx0.368. Thus a bootstrap dataset of size n contains about 63.2\% of the original observations at least once in the large- n limit. Size and number of unique rows are different quantities. Bootstrap samples contain repeated observations and omit others. Each resampled dataset is used to fit a separate model. Regularization · PDF p. 21 For regression, average the component predictions. For classification, combine class probabilities or use majority voting. Prediction aggregation is separate from fitting the component models. Step by step Derive the out-of-bag probability and expected number of unique observations Setting. Draw n indices independently and uniformly with replacement from n original observations. This is the ordinary size- n bootstrap, not sampling without replacement. 1 · Follow one particular observation At one draw, its selection probability is 1/n , so its omission probability is 1-1/n . Independence of the draws makes omission from the complete bootstrap sample P(\text{omitted})=\prod_{j=1}^n\left(1-\frac1n\right)=\left(1-\frac1n\right)^n. 2 · Take the large-sample limit carefully Take logarithms: \log P=n\log(1-1/n). Using \log(1-u)=-u-u^2/2+O(u^3) near zero, n\log(1-1/n)=-1-\frac1{2n}+O(n^{-2})\longrightarrow-1. Exponentiating gives P\to e^{-1}\approx0.367879 . For finite n , the exact formula, not e^{-1} , is the probability. At n=1 it is zero. 3 · Count unique observations with indicators Let I_i=1 if original observation i appears at least once. The unique count is U=\sum_iI_i . Linearity of expectation does not require the indicators to be independent: \mathbb E[U]=\sum_i\mathbb E[I_i]=n\left[1-\left(1-\frac1n\right)^n\right]. Thus the expected included fraction tends to 1-e^{-1}\approx0.632121 , even though the sample contains exactly n draws. 4 · Interpret out-of-bag predictions with their training boundary For each observation, aggregate only models whose bootstrap training sample omitted it. This yields an out-of-bag prediction under the ensemble construction. It does not automatically protect against preprocessing fitted using that observation, dependent entities, or future information. A temporal block bootstrap preserves some local dependence but does not by itself turn an OOB estimate into a chronological forecasting test. Derive the variance of an average At a fixed input, assume the fitted predictions have common variance \sigma^2 and pairwise correlation \rho over fitting randomness. The same covariance applies to errors relative to the fixed conditional mean, excluding fresh shared observation noise. Then \operatorname{Var}\left(\frac1M\sum_m\hat f_m\right) =\frac1{M^2}\left[M\sigma^2+M(M-1)\rho\sigma^2\right]. There are M variance terms and M(M-1) ordered covariance terms. Simplifying, \operatorname{Var}(\bar f)=\sigma^2\left[\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{M}\right]. At zero correlation, the familiar 1/M reduction appears. At perfect positive correlation, the variance does not fall at all. With a fixed positive common correlation, the limit is \rho\sigma^2 . The equal-variance/equal-correlation assumptions make this a clean explanatory model, not a literal formula for every ensemble. It explains why useful diversity of errors matters more than the number of differently named models. Variance of an ensemble average under equal component variances and a common pairwise correlation. Positive correlation leaves a variance floor as the ensemble grows. Regularization · PDF p. 22 Step by step Expand every covariance term in the variance of an average Setting. At a fixed input, let F_1,\ldots,F_M be predictions varying over model fitting. Assume all have variance \sigma^2 and distinct pairs have covariance \rho\sigma^2 . Equivalently, use errors relative to the fixed true conditional mean. Do not add an independent new-outcome noise term to each error and then count that shared noise as reducible model variance. 1 · Center the average Let \bar F=M^{-1}\sum_mF_m and \mu_m=\mathbb E[F_m] . Then \bar F-\mathbb E[\bar F]=\frac1M\sum_m(F_m-\mu_m). 2 · Expand the square as a double sum \operatorname{Var}(\bar F)=\frac1{M^2}\sum_{i=1}^M\sum_{j=1}^M \mathbb E[(F_i-\mu_i)(F_j-\mu_j)]. There are M diagonal terms with i=j , each equal to \sigma^2 . There are M(M-1) ordered off-diagonal terms, each equal to \rho\sigma^2 . Counting ordered pairs is why no extra factor of two is needed. 3 · Simplify the sum \operatorname{Var}(\bar F)=\frac{M\sigma^2+M(M-1)\rho\sigma^2}{M^2} =\sigma^2\left[\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{M}\right]. If \rho=0 , variance is \sigma^2/M . If \rho=1 , averaging changes nothing. For M=10 and \rho=0.2 , it is \sigma^2(0.2+0.8/10)=0.28\sigma^2 . 4 · Check which correlations are possible The equicorrelation matrix is (1-\rho)I+\rho\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top . Along \mathbf1 its eigenvalue is 1+(M-1)\rho ; in directions orthogonal to \mathbf1 it is 1-\rho . A covariance matrix must be positive semidefinite, so for M>1 , -\frac1{M-1}\le\rho\le1. A fixed negative correlation cannot persist unchanged as M grows without bound. The often-quoted nonzero limiting floor assumes a feasible fixed nonnegative \rho . 5 · Return to prediction error Variance reduction is only one term of squared prediction risk. Biased models can retain shared bias after averaging, and independent future observation noise remains irreducible. Diversity is useful when it lowers the relevant error covariance without making the component predictions excessively poor. Why unstable trees benefit Deep decision trees can be unstable: a small sample change may alter an early split and many predictions below it. Bagging reduces some of this variability by averaging trees fitted to different bootstrap samples. A random forest adds feature randomization when considering each split. That makes it harder for every tree to repeatedly choose the same strongest feature and can reduce correlation among trees. The motivation follows directly from the variance formula. Randomness that lowers useful signal too much would not be an improvement; the bias and diversity effects must be considered together. Out-of-bag predictions For observation i , use only models whose bootstrap samples omitted it: \hat y_i^{\mathrm{OOB}}=\frac1{|M_i|}\sum_{m\in M_i}\hat f_m(x_i). Each observation is evaluated by models that did not train on it. This can supply an internal generalization estimate for ordinary bootstrap ensembles in appropriate IID settings. The number of available out-of-bag models differs by observation; with very few models, some observations may have poor coverage. OOB evaluation is not automatically equivalent to an untouched final test after unrestricted model selection. It is a measurement within a particular resampling procedure. Why temporal data need different reasoning Ordinary row-wise resampling assumes observations are exchangeable enough for that procedure. Resampling a time series independently can destroy dependence and allow future regimes to influence models used to score earlier observations. Time-aware alternatives include block/stationary bootstrap or explicitly ordered ensembles. Preserving blocks addresses some dependence, but does not by itself enforce forecasting chronology: evaluation must still prevent future information from entering a model used to predict an earlier outcome.

title: Averaging, covariance weights, and stacking
summary: An ensemble combines predictions. Its benefit depends on the quality, bias, and covariance of its components, as well as how the combination is selected.
search:
Simple and weighted averages For M component predictions, simple averaging is \hat y=M^{-1}\sum_m\hat y_m . Weighted averaging uses \hat y=\sum_mw_m\hat y_m,\qquad\sum_mw_m=1. Select combination weights from validation or out-of-fold predictions. Nonnegativity constraints can improve stability. These weights are model-selection choices, so the final test set must remain excluded. Combining models of similar quality can help when their errors differ. Combining two nearly identical errors usually adds little. Combining a very weak predictor can also hurt, even if it is different. Covariance determines the variance of the combination Let the prediction-error covariance matrix be \Sigma . Highly correlated predictions can make the covariance estimate ill-conditioned and the weights unstable. These limitations follow from the stated quadratic problem; the formula is not a blanket recommendation to invert an empirical covariance matrix and trust the result. If the component errors have different biases, minimizing variance alone is not the same as minimizing total prediction error. Stacking learns a combination function Stacking trains a meta-model \hat y=g(\hat y_1,\ldots,\hat y_M). The base predictions act as input features. title: Architectures as information flow
summary: An architecture determines which inputs can interact, how information is carried forward, and where it is compressed. Different structures impose different assumptions about the data.
search: Separate structure, routing, and objective Architecture selection involves three choices: data structure, information flow, and prediction objective. Models can minimize the same loss while allowing very different interactions between inputs. A sequence contains meaningful order. A graph specifies relations that are not generally a simple sequence. A vector or image can be compressed through a latent representation. The appropriate architecture encodes assumptions about which interactions should be easy to represent. Recurrence carries information through a state, attention retrieves it from selected positions, and graph layers pass it along edges. A latent bottleneck instead constrains the representation through which information must pass. Comparison by information flow Family Routing mechanism Persistent or intermediate representation RNN Reuse a state transition across time Hidden state LSTM / GRU Gate the state update Cell/hidden state or one gated state Encoder–decoder Encode a source, decode a target Context or source memory Autoencoder Compress and reconstruct Latent code Transformer Content-dependent token interaction Contextual token representations GNN Pass messages along edges Node representations GAT Learn weights over graph neighbors Attention-weighted node representations There is no strict hierarchy in which each newer family replaces all earlier ones. The models express different inductive biases, and some solve different training objectives altogether. Choose the architecture by the available relationships For a streaming sequence, a recurrent state naturally carries information from the past. A bidirectional recurrent model uses future context too; that can be useful offline and invalid when future inputs are unavailable at prediction time. For a long sequence with content-dependent interactions, attention offers direct access to allowed source positions. The cost of dense pairwise interactions grows with sequence length, so the routing benefit comes with a computational trade-off. For relational data, a graph model uses the given neighborhood rather than flattening every entity into unrelated rows. Its usefulness depends on graph construction, edge direction, self-loops, and whether the split matches deployment. An autoencoder is appropriate when reconstruction or a latent representation is the objective. If labels for a downstream task are available, good reconstruction does not automatically mean the representation is best for that task. Roles can be combined Architectural roles can be combined. An LSTM autoencoder couples recurrent sequence processing with reconstruction; a temporal GNN combines state over time with relational updates. Graph Transformers and encoders followed by graph layers combine attention or representation learning with graph structure. A residual connection and an LSTM cell path share an optimization theme: preserve a relatively direct route and learn modifications around it. Gates and attention both select information, but at different granularities. A gate scales state coordinates; attention assigns weights across candidate source representations. Every autoencoder has an encoder, but a classifier’s encoder does not make it an autoencoder. Distinguishing architectural roles from training objectives separates how information is processed from what training rewards. Complexity is not just parameter count Two models with similar parameter counts can have very different computational structure. Recurrence has a sequential dependency chain. Dense attention has pairwise interactions and parallel training across positions. Graph models operate on the selected edges and can create a different batching problem for variable-size graphs. Compare architectures under the same split and metric, accounting for data volume, training time, inference cost, and robustness. Extra capacity is valuable only when it improves the intended prediction procedure at an acceptable cost. Step by step Derive receptive reach from repeated local information routing Setting. Let A be a nonnegative adjacency matrix describing allowed one-step messages between n positions or nodes. Ignore nonlinearities for the first calculation so the support of information flow is easy to inspect. This is a structural derivation, not a claim that every allowed influence is learned or useful. 1 · Expand one and two propagation steps For scalar input features x , one step gives h^{(1)}=Ax , with h^{(1)}_i=\sum_jA_{ij}x_j . Equal parameter counts therefore do not imply equal memory use, sequential depth, or runtime. Convolutional components Convolutional layers can be used inside encoders and decoders as well as classifiers. title: Recurrent networks and backpropagation through time
summary: A recurrent network reuses a state-transition function across a sequence. Backpropagation through time differentiates this unrolled computation and accumulates gradients for the shared parameters.

A state transition reused across time A vanilla RNN introduces a hidden state h_t : a_t=W_xx_t+W_hh_{t-1}+b_h,\qquad h_t=\phi(a_t),\qquad y_t=W_yh_t+b_y. The same parameters are reused at each step. Unrolling the network makes a long computation graph but does not create a separate set of recurrent weights for every time position. Parameter sharing is part of the sequential inductive bias. The hidden state is a task-shaped summary of earlier inputs. It is not guaranteed to store a human-readable record, nor to preserve every detail. Training rewards the aspects of history that help reduce the chosen loss. These tasks share the recurrent mechanism but differ in output structure and loss placement. If a loss is applied at each time step, the shared parameters receive contributions through many paths. If a loss is applied only at the end, earlier inputs must influence the final state sufficiently to receive useful credit. Sequence classification and tagging Character-level name classification uses a sequence to produce one class prediction. Part-of-speech tagging instead produces an output for each token. title: LSTM gates and memory timescales
summary: An LSTM separates cell memory from the exposed hidden state. Forget, input, and output gates control how information is retained, written, and passed onward.
search: Two states with different roles An LSTM introduces a cell state c_t in addition to the hidden output h_t . The cell provides an additive route for storing and modifying information. The hidden state exposes a gated transformation of that cell to the rest of the network. For concatenated input u_t=[h_{t-1};x_t] , the gate and state updates are f_t=\sigma(W_fu_t+b_f),\qquad i_t=\sigma(W_iu_t+b_i), \tilde c_t=\tanh(W_cu_t+b_c),\qquad c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\tilde c_t, o_t=\sigma(W_ou_t+b_o),\qquad h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t). The forget gate retains or attenuates old cell content. The input gate controls new candidate content. The output gate controls how much transformed cell content is exposed as the hidden state. These sigmoid-valued gates are continuous controls, not discrete instructions or class probabilities. Why the additive path matters A vanilla recurrent state repeatedly passes through a full nonlinear transformation. The LSTM cell instead contains a direct additive term from the previous cell. For a standard cell without peepholes, hold the previous hidden-state coordinate h_{t-1} fixed while differentiating the cell-state coordinate. The direct block is \left.\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}}\right|_{h_{t-1}\ \mathrm{fixed}}=\operatorname{diag}(f_t). Over several steps, that particular direct path scales coordinatewise as a product of the realized forget gates. When those values stay close to one, the path can retain useful sensitivity rather than repeatedly crush it through saturation. This direct cell-state block is not the total derivative of the recurrent system. Gate values depend on recurrent variables, creating additional paths through the hidden state. The full Jacobian must account for both the cell and hidden coordinates. Retention under a constant forget gate. Values close to one preserve more of an earlier cell contribution; actual forget gates vary with input and state. Architectures · PDF p. 10 Step by step Derive the direct cell-state path and the full state Jacobian Setting. Consider a standard LSTM without peephole connections. At a fixed input, gates f,i,o and candidate g depend on the previous hidden state h , while c'=f(h)\odot c+i(h)\odot g(h),\qquad h'=o(h)\odot\tanh(c'). Treat previous cell c and hidden state h as independent coordinates of the recurrent state s=(c,h) when forming its local Jacobian. 1 · Hold the hidden-state coordinate fixed If h is fixed, the gate values do not change when c changes. For coordinates j,k , \frac{\partial c'_j}{\partial c_k}=f_j\,\mathbf1_{j=k}. Therefore the direct cell-to-cell block is F=\operatorname{diag}(f) , not the vector f itself. 2 · Include the routes through the gates Let J_f=\partial f/\partial h , with analogous definitions for i,g,o . The product rule gives A=\frac{\partial c'}{\partial h} =\operatorname{diag}(c)J_f+\operatorname{diag}(g)J_i+\operatorname{diag}(i)J_g. These terms exist because changing the previous hidden state changes forgetting, writing, and candidate content. 3 · Differentiate the exposed hidden state Let T=\operatorname{diag}(o\odot[1-\tanh^2(c')]) . Then \frac{\partial h'}{\partial c}=TF, \frac{\partial h'}{\partial h}=TA+\operatorname{diag}(\tanh(c'))J_o. The first contribution passes through the updated cell; the second passes directly through the output gate. 4 · Assemble the full transition Jacobian \frac{\partial(c',h')}{\partial(c,h)}= \begin{bmatrix} F&A\\ TF&TA+\operatorname{diag}(\tanh(c'))J_o \end{bmatrix}. Across time, gradients involve products of these full block matrices. The product of forget gates describes one additive cell path, not the entire derivative of the recurrent computation. 5 · Interpret the benefit without overclaiming Along the direct path, factors near one can preserve sensitivity without repeatedly multiplying by an arbitrary recurrent matrix and a tanh derivative. This eases a particular source of vanishing gradients. Other paths, saturation, gate dynamics, and optimization still matter, so an LSTM does not guarantee nonvanishing total gradients or unlimited memory. Read a memory timescale from the gate For an approximately constant scalar forget gate f , old content contributes proportionally to f^k after k steps, before new content and other paths are considered. A value of 0.99 decays far more slowly than 0.5 . Different hidden coordinates can learn different gate values and therefore different effective timescales. This is more informative than saying an LSTM “remembers long-term information”: it learns what to retain, overwrite, and expose, coordinate by coordinate and step by step. Each write is discounted by the forget gates encountered after it was written. 2 · Solve a constant-gate retention question If all f_j=f with 0<f<1 , a write retained for k transitions is multiplied by f^k . To retain fraction r\in(0,1) , solve f^k=r\quad\Rightarrow\quad k\log f=\log r\quad\Rightarrow\quad k=\frac{\log r}{\log f}. The half-life is k_{1/2}=\log(1/2)/\log f : approximately 1 step for f=0.5 , 6.58 for 0.9 , and 68.97 for 0.99 . This is a direct-path timescale, not an empirical memory guarantee. 3 · Differentiate the local gate operations Suppose the incoming reverse gradients are \bar h_t through h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t) and \bar c_t^{\mathrm{other}} through other downstream cell routes. Add their contributions: \bar c_t=\bar c_t^{\mathrm{other}}+\bar h_t\odot o_t\odot[1-\tanh^2(c_t)]. The elementwise product rule then gives \bar f_t=\bar c_t\odot c_{t-1},\quad \bar i_t=\bar c_t\odot g_t,\quad \bar g_t=\bar c_t\odot i_t, \bar o_t=\bar h_t\odot\tanh(c_t),\qquad \bar c_{t-1}^{\mathrm{direct}}=\bar c_t\odot f_t. 4 · Continue through each gate nonlinearity For sigmoid gate pre-activations a_f,a_i,a_o and tanh candidate a_g , \bar a_f=\bar f_t\odot f_t\odot(1-f_t),\quad \bar a_i=\bar i_t\odot i_t\odot(1-i_t), \bar a_o=\bar o_t\odot o_t\odot(1-o_t),\quad \bar a_g=\bar g_t\odot(1-g_t^2). Their affine weight gradients are outer products of these signals with the corresponding concatenated input. Their contributions to h_{t-1} are summed. The exposed hidden value is smaller than the cell value because it passes through tanh and the output gate. Confusing c_t with h_t hides this distinction. Parameter counts and library conventions With input width d_x and hidden width d_h , a concatenated formulation with one bias per gate has approximately 4d_h(d_x+d_h+1) parameters before output layers. There are four affine maps: three gates plus a candidate transformation. A standard unprojected, single-layer, single-direction nn.LSTM stores separate input and recurrent biases. With biases enabled, its count is 4d_h(d_x+d_h+2) . The extra bias vectors explain the difference from the single-bias formulation. Stacking, bidirectionality, and projection layers change the count further. Step by step Count recurrent weights and distinguish one bias from two Setting. A single unidirectional, unprojected LSTM layer has input width d and hidden width h . It computes four affine transformations: input, forget, candidate, and output. 1 · Count one transformation in the mathematical convention A transformation of concatenated [h_{t-1};x_t]\in\mathbb R^{h+d} to h outputs has h(h+d) weights and h biases. Four transformations therefore have 4[h(h+d)+h]=4h(d+h+1) parameters in the single-bias formulation. 2 · Count the tensors in the PyTorch convention For one layer, the input weight tensor has shape (4h,d) and contains 4hd values. The recurrent weight tensor has shape (4h,h) and contains 4h^2 values. With biases enabled, two bias vectors each have length 4h . Hence N=4hd+4h^2+8h=4h(d+h+2). Adding the two bias vectors is functionally equivalent to one effective bias, but the library stores two trainable tensors. 3 · Verify a small example For d=3,h=5 , the four counts are 60 , 100 , 20 , and 20 , totaling 200 . The single-bias mathematical count is 4(5)(3+5+1)=180 . The difference is the additional 20 -element bias vector. 4 · State what is outside this formula An output head adds its own parameters. Stacked layers receive the previous layer’s output width; bidirectionality changes that width and adds a second direction; an LSTM projection changes recurrent shapes and adds projection weights. Sequence length and batch size do not multiply the number of shared parameters. The vanilla RNN and GRU analogues replace four affine blocks with one and three, respectively, under the same assumptions. Where the architecture is appropriate LSTMs are useful candidates for moderate-length sequences, forecasting, biosignals, speech, and streaming tasks. A bidirectional LSTM uses both past and future context, so it is unsuitable when those future observations are unavailable at inference. The part-of-speech tagging example produces a prediction at each sequence position. The time-sequence example predicts values over time. In both cases, the required memory and the information available at prediction time determine how state is passed through the model.

title: GRUs and gate conventions
summary: A GRU uses reset and update gates to modify a single hidden state. The placement of the reset gate and the meaning of the update coefficient depend on the exact formulation.
search: A compact gated state The GRU combines the roles of the LSTM’s cell and hidden state into one principal recurrent state. It uses an update gate z_t and a reset gate r_t : z_t=\sigma(W_zx_t+U_zh_{t-1}+b_z), r_t=\sigma(W_rx_t+U_rh_{t-1}+b_r), \tilde h_t=\tanh(W_hx_t+U_h(r_t\odot h_{t-1})+b_h), h_t=(1-z_t)\odot h_{t-1}+z_t\odot\tilde h_t. In this candidate-weighted convention , a larger update gate moves the state more strongly toward the candidate. The reset gate controls how previous-state information enters the candidate computation. The final interpolation creates an additive route between old and new information. That is the connection to LSTM memory-path reasoning, despite the different state organization. A scalar state update Let h_{t-1}=0.6 , z_t=0.25 , and the already-computed candidate be \tilde h_t=-0.2 . Then h_t=0.75(0.6)+0.25(-0.2)=0.40. The small candidate weight keeps most of the old state. The reset gate was used to construct the candidate; once that candidate is known, the reset value does not enter the final interpolation again. This separates two questions: how to construct the candidate, and how strongly to replace the state with it. Compare GRU and LSTM models under the same split, training conditions, and constraints on prediction-time information. PyTorch’s documented convention PyTorch weights the previous hidden state with the update gate: h_t=(1-z_t)\odot n_t+z_t\odot h_{t-1}. Here a large z_t preserves the old state. Since n and z_s themselves depend on h , the total state Jacobian contains additional chain-rule terms. 3 · Compare the reset placement A common textbook candidate uses U(r\odot h)=U\operatorname{diag}(r)h . PyTorch’s candidate uses r\odot(Uh+b_h)=\operatorname{diag}(r)(Uh+b_h) . Its single-layer, unidirectional bias-enabled parameter count is 3h(d+h+2) , because it stores three input/recurrent affine blocks and two bias vectors per block. A GRU decoder updates its own state while producing outputs, optionally using attention to retrieve encoder states. title: Encoders, decoders, and teacher forcing
summary: An encoder constructs a representation; a decoder turns it into an output. Autoregressive decoding conditions each prediction on earlier outputs, with different available histories during training and inference.
search: Encoder and decoder describe roles An encoder transforms an input into a useful representation. A decoder transforms a representation into an output. Either can use recurrent layers, attention, convolutions, or graph computations. The label specifies information flow, not a particular neuron or layer. In classical recurrent sequence-to-sequence modeling, the encoder processes x_{1:T} into context c . The decoder models p(y_{1:U}\mid x_{1:T})=\prod_{u=1}^{U}p(y_u\mid y_{<u},c). The input and output lengths can differ. At each output step, the model conditions on source information and earlier target tokens. This is different from requiring one output aligned with every input position. Why the autoregressive factorization is useful Rather than produce a whole structured sequence as an unstructured object, the model makes a series of conditional predictions. For observed target sequence y^* , the usual token-level negative log-likelihood is L=-\sum_{u=1}^{U}\log p(y_u^*\mid y_{<u}^*,c). The model is trained to assign high probability to each observed token under the conditioning history. The chosen representation, decoder state, and attention mechanism determine how it uses that context. In translation, each generated word depends on the encoded input and the words already produced. The decoder therefore models a sequence of conditional distributions rather than independent output words. Step by step Derive the autoregressive likelihood and masked token loss Setting. Let x be an observed source sequence and y_1,\ldots,y_U a target sequence, including an end-of-sequence token when termination is modeled. No independence between target tokens is assumed. 1 · Apply the conditional probability product rule For two target tokens, p(y_1,y_2\mid x)=p(y_1\mid x)p(y_2\mid y_1,x). Applying the same rule to a third gives a new factor p(y_3\mid y_1,y_2,x) . Repeating yields p_\theta(y_{1:U}\mid x)=\prod_{u=1}^U p_\theta(y_u\mid y_{<u},x). This factorization is a probability identity. An encoder–decoder supplies a parameterization of its factors; a compressed context may impose an approximation to the full conditioning information. 2 · Convert a product into an additive training objective Take negative natural logarithms: -\log p_\theta(y_{1:U}\mid x)=-\sum_{u=1}^U\log p_\theta(y_u\mid y_{<u},x). The target history in each factor is the observed history. Supplying it during training is teacher forcing, consistent with evaluating the likelihood of the observed sequence. 3 · Expand one categorical token loss For logits z_{u,k} over vocabulary classes k and observed token y_u , -\log p_\theta(y_u\mid y_{<u},x) =-z_{u,y_u}+\log\sum_k e^{z_{u,k}}. The decoder must receive shifted targets or a mask that prevents the token at u from directly revealing its own answer. 4 · Remove padding without changing the modeled event For a padded batch, let m_{b,u}=1 for genuine target tokens and zero for padding. A mean per-token objective is J=\frac{\sum_{b,u}m_{b,u}\ell_{b,u}}{\sum_{b,u}m_{b,u}}. This requires at least one valid token. Averaging each sequence separately and then averaging sequences gives a different weighting when lengths differ. Both may be deliberate, but the denominator must match the intended objective. 5 · Explain generation separately At generation time, the true prefix is unavailable. The model conditions on generated tokens and chooses or samples the next token until termination. Sampling implements the autoregressive model; greedy or beam decoding is a decision procedure over that model. Parallel teacher-forced training does not make ordinary autoregressive generation nonsequential. Teacher forcing During training, true previous tokens are available, so the decoder can receive y_{u-1}^* . This is teacher forcing. At inference it cannot receive an unknown true target token, so it receives its own previous prediction instead. The resulting mismatch is exposure bias : training histories are often cleaner than the histories encountered after an error during free-running generation. This does not make teacher forcing invalid; it identifies a difference between the conditional training calculation and the generation procedure. Teacher forcing also does not give permission to include unavailable future target information. The autoregressive structure still determines which context each prediction is allowed to use. The fixed-context bottleneck An early recurrent encoder–decoder might compress the entire input into one final state. For a long source sequence, that fixed-width representation must carry every detail the decoder will later need. Attention relieves this bottleneck by letting each decoder step retrieve from all encoder states. With additive attention, e_{u,t}=v^\top\tanh(W_ss_{u-1}+W_hh_t), \alpha_{u,t}=\frac{e^{e_{u,t}}}{\sum_j e^{e_{u,j}}},\qquad c_u=\sum_t\alpha_{u,t}h_t. Now the context is specific to output step u . The decoder can emphasize different source positions at different stages instead of relying exclusively on one fixed vector. Three architectural forms An encoder-only model contextualizes the available input and can support classification, tagging, retrieval, or embeddings. A decoder-only model uses allowed prior context for autoregressive generation. An encoder–decoder model builds source memory and then generates while consulting it. These are routing forms that can appear with recurrent components or Transformers. “Encoder” is not a synonym for “autoencoder”: reconstruction is a particular training objective discussed in the next chapter. Translation with additive attention The translation example below combines a GRU encoder and decoder with teacher forcing and additive attention. Its attention maps show which encoder positions contribute to the context at each output step. During training, identify where true target tokens enter the decoder. During generation, trace how earlier predictions become new inputs. In both modes, the attention weights determine the context vector retrieved from the encoder states.

title: Autoencoders, bottlenecks, and denoising
summary: An autoencoder learns a representation by reconstructing its input. Bottlenecks, sparsity, and denoising constrain the solution so that reconstruction requires more than copying.
search: Reconstruction defines the task An autoencoder uses an encoder and decoder with the input itself as the usual target: z=f_\theta(x),\qquad\hat x=g_\phi(z). The encoder constructs a code z and the decoder reconstructs the observation. This is not simply “an encoder model”; the paired reconstruction objective is essential to the definition. An encoder maps the input to a latent code; a decoder reconstructs it. Useful compression depends on the bottleneck or training constraints, not just on having an encoder–decoder structure. Architectures · PDF p. 15 For continuous data, a common objective is squared reconstruction error, for example \lVert x-\hat x\rVert^2/d . For binary or Bernoulli-modeled inputs, a binary cross-entropy reconstruction objective can be appropriate. The likelihood assumptions and feature scales matter. A bottleneck restricts the easy identity map If the latent dimension k is smaller than input dimension d , the autoencoder is undercomplete. It must prioritize information that helps reconstruction. But dimension alone does not guarantee useful semantics: a powerful nonlinear model can still memorize a finite training sample or devote its limited capacity to nuisance variation. With an undercomplete linear encoder and decoder, squared reconstruction loss is related to the principal subspace of PCA. The optimal reconstruction subspace need not give latent axes with the same orientation or interpretation as a particular PCA basis. A nonlinear decoder can represent curved structure, but additional expressiveness also changes the risks. Good training reconstruction is not enough to establish a useful general representation. Step by step Derive the PCA connection for a linear reconstruction model Setting. Use centered column-vector data x\in\mathbb R^d with finite second moment S=\mathbb E[xx^\top] . Consider an orthogonal rank- k linear reconstruction \hat x=UU^\top x , where U\in\mathbb R^{d\times k} and U^\top U=I . This restricted problem makes the principal-subspace connection explicit. 1 · Expand the reconstruction error Let P=UU^\top . Since P^\top=P and P^2=P , \|x-Px\|^2=x^\top(I-P)^\top(I-P)x=x^\top(I-P)x. The last equality follows from (I-P)^2=I-2P+P^2=I-P . 2 · Take the expectation using a trace For a scalar, x^\top Ax=\operatorname{tr}(Axx^\top) . Therefore \mathbb E\|x-Px\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(S)-\operatorname{tr}(PS) =\operatorname{tr}(S)-\operatorname{tr}(U^\top SU). The first term is constant. Minimizing error is equivalent to maximizing variance captured by the k -dimensional subspace. 3 · Rotate into covariance eigenvectors Write S=V\Lambda V^\top , with eigenvalues \lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\ge0 , and put C=V^\top U . Then C^\top C=I and \operatorname{tr}(U^\top SU)=\operatorname{tr}(C^\top\Lambda C) =\sum_{i=1}^d\lambda_i\sum_{j=1}^k C_{ij}^2. Let a_i=\sum_jC_{ij}^2 . Because CC^\top is an orthogonal projector, 0\le a_i\le1 and \sum_i a_i=k . 4 · Allocate captured dimensions to the largest eigenvalues For ordered eigenvalues, the largest possible weighted sum under those constraints is \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i : if weight remains on a smaller eigenvalue while a larger one has available capacity, transferring that weight cannot reduce the sum. Choosing U as the first k eigenvectors attains this bound. Thus the minimum reconstruction error is \sum_{i=k+1}^d\lambda_i . 5 · Avoid claiming unique latent coordinates For unconstrained linear encoder/decoder matrices, the principal reconstruction subspace can be represented in many latent bases. Replacing an encoder by RE and decoder by DR^{-1} for invertible R leaves DE unchanged. An ordinary nonlinear autoencoder therefore neither guarantees PCA coordinates nor solves this exact orthogonal projection problem. The equivalence concerns the optimal linear squared-error reconstruction subspace under appropriate conditions. Denoising changes the shortcut A denoising autoencoder sees a corrupted input but reconstructs the clean target: \tilde x\sim q(\tilde x\mid x),\qquad L=\lVert x-g_\phi(f_\theta(\tilde x))\rVert^2. Copying the noisy input is no longer sufficient. The model is encouraged to preserve stable structure that predicts the clean sample. This only makes sense if the corruption process represents a valid nuisance rather than changes that should alter the desired target. For example, reconstructing a clean signal from a plausible noisy measurement has a clear interpretation. Adding arbitrary noise to strongly constrained features can instead create unrealistic training examples. The augmentation and noise chapter develops that assumption. Step by step Derive the optimal denoising reconstruction under squared error Setting. Let clean data be a random vector X and corrupted input be Z . Train a reconstruction function g by minimizing \mathbb E\|X-g(Z)\|^2 . Assume the relevant conditional second moments exist. The function class is unrestricted for this population argument. 1 · Condition on a particular corrupted observation At Z=z , a proposed reconstruction a=g(z) incurs conditional risk \mathbb E[\|X-a\|^2\mid Z=z] . Define \mu(z)=\mathbb E[X\mid Z=z] . 2 · Add and subtract the conditional mean X-a=[X-\mu(z)]+[\mu(z)-a]. Expanding the squared norm gives \|X-a\|^2=\|X-\mu(z)\|^2+\|\mu(z)-a\|^2 +2[X-\mu(z)]^\top[\mu(z)-a]. 3 · Evaluate the cross term Given Z=z , the vector \mu(z)-a is fixed and \mathbb E[X-\mu(z)\mid Z=z]=0 . Thus the expected cross term is zero, and \mathbb E[\|X-a\|^2\mid z]=\mathbb E[\|X-\mu(z)\|^2\mid z]+\|\mu(z)-a\|^2. Only the last term depends on a , and it is minimized at a=\mu(z) . 4 · Read the consequence for a denoising model The population optimum is g^*(z)=\mathbb E[X\mid Z=z] . If corruption makes several clean inputs plausible, squared-error training averages them. A blurred reconstruction can therefore follow from ambiguity and the chosen loss, not only inadequate model capacity. 5 · State the limits of the result A finite neural network, finite training sample, or imperfect optimizer may not reach this optimum. The corruption distribution determines the conditional mean being learned. Denoising success does not alone certify anomaly detection, class separation, or a useful causal representation. Sparse and overcomplete codes A sparse autoencoder can provide many latent units while penalizing frequent activation. A KL penalty on mean hidden activity constrains use of the code rather than simply its dimensionality. This is different from dropout’s random temporary masks and from an L1 penalty on network weights. Each acts on a different object in the learning system. Anomaly detection is conditional on reconstruction behavior One approach trains primarily on normal observations and scores s(x)=\lVert x-\hat x\rVert^2 . A high score can flag observations that are poorly represented by the learned reconstruction system. Illustrative reconstruction-error distributions for typical and atypical observations. Their overlap creates a trade-off between missed anomalies and false positives when selecting a threshold. Architectures · PDF p. 16 The key assumption is that anomalous observations reconstruct substantially worse than normal observations. An overly expressive autoencoder can reconstruct anomalies too well, and normal distribution shifts can also raise scores. A threshold therefore needs validation and a connection to the relevant false-positive or downstream cost. A denoising example The denoising example trains on a corrupted synthetic curve with clean reconstruction targets. It keeps validation corruption fixed, selects a checkpoint on held-out validation data, and evaluates test data afterward. The example demonstrates denoising rather than validating an anomaly detector. The VAE implementation below is a separate probabilistic extension. A variational autoencoder changes this construction by introducing a latent distribution, a decoder likelihood, and a KL term in a probabilistic training objective.

title: Variational autoencoders and the ELBO
summary: A variational autoencoder learns a latent-variable generative model. Its encoder approximates the posterior, and its objective balances reconstruction likelihood with divergence from a latent prior.
search:
Replace a point code with a conditional distribution A deterministic autoencoder assigns a code to an input. A VAE encoder parameterizes an approximate posterior, commonly q_\phi(z\mid x)=\mathcal N\left(\mu_\phi(x),\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_\phi^2(x))ight). The latent prior is often p(z)=\mathcal N(0,I) , and a decoder specifies a likelihood p_	heta(x\mid z) . The goal is not merely to reconstruct one point through a noisy layer; it is to learn a latent-variable generative model with a tractable approximation to inference. The evidence lower bound The evidence lower bound, or ELBO, is \mathcal L_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)=\mathbb E_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}[\log p_	heta(x\mid z)] -\operatorname{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\Vert p(z)). Training minimizes the negative ELBO, equivalently maximizing this lower bound. The expectation rewards likelihood of the observed input under latent samples. The KL term pulls the approximate posterior toward the chosen prior. A “reconstruction loss” is therefore a negative log-likelihood term under a particular observation model, not an arbitrary interchangeable distance. The decoder’s output distribution determines what loss is consistent with it. Why the ELBO is a lower bound Introduce q_\phi(z\mid x) and rewrite \log p_	heta(x)=\mathcal L_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)+ \operatorname{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\Vert p_	heta(z\mid x)). The last term is nonnegative, so the ELBO cannot exceed the log evidence. Equality holds when the approximate posterior matches the model posterior, subject to the usual distribution/support conditions. Expanding the ELBO expectation as \mathbb E_q[\log p_	heta(x,z)-\log q_\phi(z\mid x)] and using p_	heta(x,z)=p_	heta(x\mid z)p(z) gives the reconstruction-likelihood and prior-divergence terms above. This separates the tractable training bound from the generally difficult exact posterior. Step by step Derive the evidence bound and identify its exact gap Setting. Fix an observed x with p_	heta(x)>0 . Let q_\phi(z\mid x) be a normalized density, with support compatible with the following ratios and finite expectations. All logarithms are natural. 1 · Introduce the latent variable and an auxiliary density Marginalization gives p_	heta(x)=\int p_	heta(x,z)\,dz . If q covers the relevant joint support, multiply and divide the integrand by q : p_	heta(x)=\int q_\phi(z\mid x) rac{p_	heta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\,dz =\mathbb E_q\left[ rac{p_	heta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}ight]. 2 · Apply concavity of the logarithm For positive R , Jensen’s inequality says \log\mathbb E[R]\ge\mathbb E[\log R] . Therefore \log p_	heta(x)\ge\mathbb E_q[\log p_	heta(x,z)-\log q_\phi(z\mid x)]\equiv\mathcal E(	heta,\phi;x). This quantity \mathcal E is the evidence lower bound, or ELBO. 3 · Factor the joint model Use p_	heta(x,z)=p_	heta(x\mid z)p(z) . Logarithms split the product: \mathcal E=\mathbb E_q[\log p_	heta(x\mid z)] +\mathbb E_q[\log p(z)-\log q_\phi(z\mid x)]. The second term is negative KL, yielding \mathcal E=\mathbb E_q[\log p_	heta(x\mid z)]- D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p(z)). 4 · Derive the gap directly using Bayes’ rule Since p_	heta(z\mid x)=p_	heta(x,z)/p_	heta(x) , D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p_	heta(z\mid x)) =\mathbb E_q[\log q-\log p_	heta(x,z)+\log p_	heta(x)]. The evidence is constant with respect to z , so this becomes D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p_	heta(z\mid x))=\log p_	heta(x)-\mathcal E. Rearranging gives an exact identity, not merely an inequality. The KL-to- posterior is the gap; the KL-to- prior is the term appearing in the decomposed training bound. They are different objects. 5 · Justify nonnegativity For normalized compatible densities q,p , concavity gives \mathbb E_q\log rac pq\le\log\mathbb E_q rac pq\le\log1=0. Negating yields D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\ge0 . Equality requires matching distributions almost everywhere. Thus the bound is tight exactly when the variational posterior matches the true posterior under the stated conditions. 6 · Convert the bound to a minimized objective Training typically minimizes -\mathcal E=\mathbb E_q[-\log p_	heta(x\mid z)]+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p(z)) . A changed coefficient on KL or an independently rescaled reconstruction loss changes this objective; it is not automatically the same model’s exact negative ELBO. Reparameterization separates randomness from parameters Directly sampling from a parameter-dependent distribution obscures an ordinary differentiable path. Reparameterization writes \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I),\qquad z=\mu_\phi(x)+\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\epsilon. The random draw now has a fixed parameter-independent distribution. For a sampled \epsilon , the transformation from \mu,\sigma to z is differentiable. A Monte Carlo estimate can then pass gradients through the decoder and into the encoder parameters. This does not eliminate sampling variation. It gives a usable gradient path for the selected distributional family. Step by step Differentiate through Gaussian reparameterization Setting. Draw \varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I) independently of model parameters. Define z=\mu_\phi(x)+\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\varepsilon . Independent noise coordinates yield diagonal covariance, so this construction samples the desired Gaussian. 2 · Rewrite the expectation over fixed base noise For a differentiable function F , the equal distributions imply \mathbb E_{z\sim q_\phi}[F(z)]=\mathbb E_\varepsilon[F(\mu_\phi+\sigma_\phi\odot\varepsilon)]. The distribution on the right does not move when \phi changes; only the transformation does. 3 · Apply the chain rule to a sampled computation Let g_j=\partial F/\partial z_j . Holding the sampled \varepsilon fixed,  rac{\partial F}{\partial\mu_j}=g_j,\qquad  rac{\partial F}{\partial\sigma_j}=g_j\varepsilon_j. abla_\phi\mu_j+\varepsilon_j
abla_\phi\sigma_jight)ight]. A sample average of the bracketed term estimates this gradient. If F also depends explicitly on \phi , its direct derivative must be added; the formula above assumes its parameter dependence is through z . 5 · Interpret the randomness correctly We do not differentiate the random-number generator. We differentiate a deterministic transformation of already sampled noise, then average over such computations. This is a pathwise gradient estimator; it does not by itself establish a valid pathwise estimator for discrete categorical sampling. Let q(z\mid x)=\mathcal N(\mu,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\ldots,\sigma_d^2)) with every \sigma_j>0 , and let p(z)=\mathcal N(0,I) . The parameters are fixed for the observed x during this calculation. 1 · Write both log densities \log q(z)=- rac d2\log(2\pi)-\sum_j\log\sigma_j - rac12\sum_j rac{(z_j-\mu_j)^2}{\sigma_j^2}, \log p(z)=- rac d2\log(2\pi)- rac12\sum_jz_j^2. 2 · Subtract to cancel the normalization constants \log rac{q(z)}{p(z)} = rac12\sum_j\left[z_j^2- rac{(z_j-\mu_j)^2}{\sigma_j^2}-\log\sigma_j^2ight]. The logarithmic term uses 2\log\sigma_j=\log\sigma_j^2 . 3 · Evaluate each expectation under q By definition, \mathbb E_q[z_j]=\mu_j and \operatorname{Var}_q(z_j)=\sigma_j^2 . Hence \mathbb E_q[z_j^2]=\sigma_j^2+\mu_j^2,\qquad \mathbb E_q[(z_j-\mu_j)^2/\sigma_j^2]=1. The log variance is constant under this expectation. 4 · Substitute and sum D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)= rac12\sum_{j=1}^d \left(\mu_j^2+\sigma_j^2-1-\log\sigma_j^2ight). For network output \ell_j=\log\sigma_j^2 , substitute \sigma_j^2=e^{\ell_j} : D_{\mathrm{KL}}= rac12\sum_j(\mu_j^2+e^{\ell_j}-1-\ell_j). Each term is nonnegative because u-1-\log u\ge0 for u>0 and \mu_j^2\ge0 . 5 · Differentiate the analytic result  rac{\partial D_{\mathrm{KL}}}{\partial\mu_j}=\mu_j,\qquad  rac{\partial D_{\mathrm{KL}}}{\partial\ell_j}= rac12(e^{\ell_j}-1). For \mu=0 and \ell=0 , the posterior equals the prior, so KL and both derivatives vanish. With \mu=1,\sigma=2 , one dimension contributes (1+4-1-\log4)/2\approx1.30685 . 6 · Keep the reduction consistent The displayed expression sums latent coordinates for one example. A batch objective may average these per-example values, while its reconstruction likelihood normally sums observed dimensions per example. Averaging one term over its dimensions but not the other changes their relative weight. Read the objective’s trade-off The encoder is pulled toward codes that support reconstruction and toward posterior distributions compatible with the prior. If the latent variable is ignored, a low KL by itself is not evidence of a useful representation. If reconstruction dominates without an appropriate prior relationship, the generative interpretation can weaken. The implementation below trains a VAE on MNIST and produces both reconstructions and samples from the latent prior. These two outputs illustrate different uses of the learned decoder.

title: Attention: queries, keys, values, and weights
summary: Attention compares queries with keys and uses the resulting weights to combine values. Scaling, masking, and multiple heads control how that information is selected.
search: Attention is content-dependent retrieval A query retrieves a weighted combination of values. Keys determine how strongly each source matches that query. The three roles are distinct even when all are projected from the same input sequence. For X\in\mathbb R^{T\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} , form Q=XW_Q , K=XW_K , and V=XW_V . Scaled dot-product attention is \operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)= \operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V. Softmax is applied across the allowed keys for each query row. The output is a mixture of values , not a mixture of keys. The score matrix determines where to retrieve; the value matrix determines what is retrieved. Shapes explain the operation If Q has T_q rows and K,V have T_k rows, then QK^\top has shape T_q\times T_k . Each query receives one score for each key. Multiplying the normalized scores by V\in\mathbb R^{T_k\times d_v} produces T_q\times d_v outputs. The number of queries need not equal the number of keys. Cross-attention can therefore connect sequences of different lengths while producing one output per query. Step by step Derive attention gradients with respect to queries, keys, and values Setting. For one head, let Q\in\mathbb R^{T\times d_k} , K\in\mathbb R^{S\times d_k} , V\in\mathbb R^{S\times d_v} . Define A=QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k} , rowwise probabilities P=\operatorname{softmax}(A) , and O=PV . Assume each row has at least one allowed key. Hold any mask fixed and ignore dropout for this derivation. Let incoming gradient G=\partial L/\partial O have shape T\times d_v . 1 · Differentiate the value mixture entry by entry O_{ib}=\sum_{j=1}^SP_{ij}V_{jb}. Thus the gradient with respect to one value element is \sum_iG_{ib}P_{ij} , and the gradient with respect to one probability is \sum_bG_{ib}V_{jb} . In matrix form, \bar V=P^\top G,\qquad \bar P=GV^\top. Their shapes are S\times d_v and T\times S . 2 · Apply the full rowwise softmax Jacobian For fixed query row i , \partial P_{ij}/\partial A_{ir}=P_{ij}(\mathbf1_{j=r}-P_{ir}) . Sum over all affected outputs in that row: \bar A_{ir}=\sum_j\bar P_{ij}P_{ij}(\mathbf1_{j=r}-P_{ir}) =P_{ir}\left[\bar P_{ir}-\sum_jP_{ij}\bar P_{ij}\right]. The bracket subtracts a probability-weighted row mean. This avoids constructing a dense S\times S Jacobian for each row. 3 · Differentiate the scaled scores A_{ij}=\frac1{\sqrt{d_k}}\sum_aQ_{ia}K_{ja}. Hence \bar Q_{ia}=\frac1{\sqrt{d_k}}\sum_j\bar A_{ij}K_{ja},\qquad \bar K_{ja}=\frac1{\sqrt{d_k}}\sum_i\bar A_{ij}Q_{ia}. Collecting entries gives \bar Q=\frac{\bar AK}{\sqrt{d_k}},\qquad \bar K=\frac{\bar A^\top Q}{\sqrt{d_k}}. 4 · Continue through shared self-attention inputs If Q=XW_Q , K=XW_K , and V=XW_V , then \bar X=\bar QW_Q^\top+\bar KW_K^\top+\bar VW_V^\top, \bar W_Q=X^\top\bar Q,\quad\bar W_K=X^\top\bar K,\quad\bar W_V=X^\top\bar V. All three branches depend on X , so their contributions must be added. Cross-attention has different query and key/value source tensors, so their gradient branches are accumulated to the appropriate source instead. 5 · Respect operations omitted from the derivation Attention dropout, output projection, residual paths, and normalization contribute additional local derivatives when present. Masked positions have no score influence when their probability is fixed at zero. This derivation verifies the elementary attention operation, not every optimized kernel or complete Transformer block. Why the square-root scale appears For the initialization-scale argument, assume independent, zero-mean query/key components with unit variance and no cross-coordinate dependence. Summing d_k products gives a dot-product variance growing with d_k . Large logits can make softmax highly concentrated and reduce useful sensitivity. Dividing by \sqrt{d_k} controls this dimension-induced scale. The assumption explains the design choice; it does not say that every trained query/key distribution is exactly independent or unit variance. Learned projections, normalization, and actual data affect the observed scores. Step by step Derive the square-root attention scale from moments Setting. Let s=q^\top k=\sum_{j=1}^{d_k}q_jk_j . For this initialization-scale argument, assume pairs across coordinates are independent; within each pair, q_j and k_j are independent, zero mean, and have variances v_q and v_k . Real learned queries and keys need not retain these assumptions. 1 · Evaluate one product’s mean Independence gives \mathbb E[q_jk_j]=\mathbb E[q_j]\mathbb E[k_j]=0 . 2 · Evaluate its second moment and variance \mathbb E[(q_jk_j)^2]=\mathbb E[q_j^2]\mathbb E[k_j^2]=v_qv_k. Since the mean is zero, this is also \operatorname{Var}(q_jk_j) . 3 · Sum the coordinate contributions \operatorname{Var}(s)=\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(q_jk_j) +\sum_{j\ne r}\operatorname{Cov}(q_jk_j,q_rk_r). Coordinate independence makes the covariance terms zero. Therefore \operatorname{Var}(s)=d_kv_qv_k . 4 · Scale the standard deviation, not the variance directly For a=s/\sqrt{d_k} , variance scales by the square of the divisor: \operatorname{Var}(a)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(s)}{d_k}=v_qv_k. With unit component variances, the scaled score has variance one. Dividing by d_k would instead make its variance 1/d_k . 5 · Connect score scale to softmax sensitivity For weights p_i=\operatorname{softmax}(s)_i , the derivative is \partial p_i/\partial s_j=p_i(\mathbf1_{i=j}-p_j) . When one score dominates and the distribution saturates, many of these derivatives approach zero. Scaling avoids a predictable increase in score magnitude with width under the stated assumptions. It is not a proof that all trained scores have unit variance or that saturation can never occur. A weighted-mixture example Take q=(1,0) and keys k_1=(1,0) , k_2=(0,1) , k_3=(1,1) . With d_k=2 , scaled scores are approximately (0.707,0,0.707) , giving weights \alpha\approx(0.401,0.198,0.401). For values v_1=(1,0) , v_2=(0,2) , and v_3=(1,1) , \alpha_1v_1+\alpha_2v_2+\alpha_3v_3\approx(0.802,0.797). The second source has a lower weight but still contributes to the second output coordinate because its value has magnitude two there. A large attention coefficient alone is not a full measure of a source’s eventual effect on a prediction. An illustrative self-attention matrix. Each row is a distribution over key positions for one query; these values are not measurements from a trained language model. Keys determine the weights; values supply the vectors being mixed. A key and its corresponding value do not have to be equal vectors. 5 · Handle a mask before normalization A disallowed position receives score -\infty and exponential zero. Normalize only over the remaining allowed positions. If all positions are disallowed, the mathematical denominator is zero and no probability distribution is defined by this formula; prevent that case or handle it explicitly according to the chosen implementation. The complete equations and worked values remain available in the calculation above. Self-attention and cross-attention In self-attention, queries, keys, and values are derived from the same sequence. In cross-attention, queries come from one sequence and keys/values from another—typically decoder states querying encoder memory. Masks restrict which sources are allowed. An autoregressive query must not retrieve forbidden future information. “Attention is global” should therefore be read as “direct access to the allowed interaction set,” not a requirement that every possible pair is used. Why use multiple heads? title: Transformers: position, residual paths, and masking
summary: Transformers combine attention, position-wise feed-forward layers, residual connections, and normalization. Position signals and attention masks determine which sequence relationships they can represent.

The output permutes in the same way as the input: equivariance , not invariance. Position embeddings, relative-position biases, recurrence, or masking can all supply order-dependent structure. An encoder–decoder decoder combines masked self-attention with cross-attention to the encoder’s source memory. An additive causal mask is M_{ij}=\begin{cases}0&j\le i\\-\infty&j>i.\end{cases} Adding it before softmax gives zero weight to disallowed future positions. Boolean mask meanings differ across APIs: scaled_dot_product_attention uses True for an allowed entry, while MultiheadAttention boolean masks use True for a blocked entry. Every query needs a valid normalization domain; an entirely masked row is not a probability distribution under the mathematical softmax formula. In the functional SDPA call, a nonzero dropout_p applies dropout even if a surrounding module is in evaluation mode, so pass zero explicitly for deterministic evaluation. Per head, Q,K,V have shape 16\times100\times32 , and the score matrix is 16\times100\times100 . Across eight heads, that is 8\times16\times100\times100=1{,}280{,}000 attention weights in the naive explicit representation. This calculation explains where the sequence-length cost arises. Optimized kernels can change memory materialization and constants without turning the conceptual dense interaction pattern into recurrence. Step by step Count tensor elements, matrix products, and projection parameters Setting. Use batch B=16 , length T=100 , model width d=256 , and H=8 heads. Split widths evenly so d_k=d_v=d/H=32 . Ignore padding and describe an ordinary dense attention implementation. 1 · Follow each shape The model representation is (B,T,d)=(16,100,256) . Each head uses Q_h,K_h,V_h with shape (16,100,32) . Multiplying Q_hK_h^\top gives (16,100,100) scores. Across heads, the score count is BHT^2=16\cdot8\cdot100\cdot100=1{,}280{,}000. Summing over heads gives BT^2Hd_k=BT^2d . Multiplying attention weights by values gives another BT^2d term. This is the origin of the O(BT^2d) interaction cost. 3 · Include the projections that the interaction shorthand omits Each of the three input projections maps d to d for every token, costing BTd^2 terms. The output projection adds one more, for roughly 4BTd^2 projection terms. Thus full attention arithmetic includes both BTd^2 and BT^2d contributions, before the feed-forward sublayer. 4 · Count trainable parameters separately Three dense d\times d input projections plus one output projection have 4d^2 weights. With one bias per projected feature in each map, add 4d biases. For d=256 , that is 262{,}144+1{,}024=263{,}168 parameters. This count does not multiply by T , B , or H when total projected width remains d . 5 · Distinguish arithmetic from materialized memory A straightforward implementation stores the quadratic score/probability arrays. The quadratic all-pairs interaction arithmetic remains distinct from this memory optimization. Actual runtime also depends on kernels, hardware, masks, and sequence lengths. Parallel work and quadratic interactions An RNN’s h_t depends on h_{t-1} , creating a sequential chain. Self-attention computes all allowed query/key interactions within a layer in parallel. Dense attention’s interaction term is O(T^2d) , while a recurrent layer has roughly O(Td_h^2) arithmetic and sequential depth O(T) in this simplified comparison. Linear growth in recurrent steps versus quadratic growth in dense pairwise interactions. Projection costs, hardware, and implementation constants also affect runtime. Architectures · PDF p. 22 Dense attention can be expensive at long sequence lengths despite its parallelism. Sparse, local, linearized, and chunked variants address this cost by changing the interactions or how they are computed. Training and generation are different computations During teacher-forced causal training, all target positions are known, so a mask permits parallel loss calculation without future leakage. During generation, new tokens must be produced before they can become inputs to later predictions. Generation remains sequential at the token level. Key/value caching avoids recomputing earlier projections at each generation step. It reduces repeated computation without removing the dependency on earlier generated tokens. Position and visibility rules are part of the architecture. A model with the wrong mask can perform the tensor operations correctly while using information that should be unavailable.

title: GNNs, graph attention, and relational bottlenecks
summary: Graph neural networks combine information across connected nodes. Neighborhood aggregation, normalization, and permutation symmetry determine how node representations are updated.
search: The input includes relationships A graph G=(V,E) specifies entities and their relations. Node neighborhoods can vary in size, and the arbitrary ordering of nodes in a file should not change what a model means. A graph network therefore needs a rule for combining variable-size neighborhoods with appropriate permutation symmetry. A message-passing layer can be written as m_i^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{AGG}_{j\in\mathcal N(i)} \psi_\ell(h_i^{(\ell)},h_j^{(\ell)},e_{ij}), h_i^{(\ell+1)}=\phi_\ell(h_i^{(\ell)},m_i^{(\ell)}). The learned transformation and nonlinear activation then produce the next representation. Step by step Calculate symmetric graph normalization, not just a neighbor mean Setting. Use an undirected three-node path 1\!- obreakdash 2\!- obreakdash 3 with no initial self-loops. Each node has scalar feature x=(2,1,4)^\top . We will add one self-loop per node and use a scalar feature weight w=0.5 followed by ReLU. 1 · Write adjacency and add self-loops A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \tilde A=A+I=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\1&1&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}. Hence S=\begin{bmatrix} 1/2&1/\sqrt6&0\\ 1/\sqrt6&1/3&1/\sqrt6\\ 0&1/\sqrt6&1/2 \end{bmatrix}. A graph classifier that changes prediction merely because rows were reordered violates the intended invariance. A node classifier must still preserve which output belongs to which node. Step by step Prove node equivariance and graph-level invariance Setting. Let node features be H and symmetrically normalized adjacency be S . A layer is F(H,A)=\sigma(SHW) with shared weights W and elementwise \sigma . Let P be a permutation matrix relabeling nodes. 1 · Relabel both features and relationships The relabeled features are H'=PH and adjacency A'=PAP^\top . Since PIP^\top=I , self-loop adjacency becomes \tilde A'=P\tilde AP^\top . Row sums reorder the degree entries, so \tilde D'=P\tilde DP^\top . 2 · Relabel normalization consistently For a positive diagonal degree matrix, taking inverse square roots reorders the same diagonal values: (\tilde D')^{-1/2}=P\tilde D^{-1/2}P^\top. Substituting into the normalized adjacency and canceling P^\top P=I gives S'=PSP^\top . 3 · Propagate and use shared elementwise operations F(H',A')=\sigma(S'H'W)=\sigma(PSP^\top PHW)=\sigma(PSHW). A row permutation commutes with the shared elementwise nonlinearity, so F(H',A')=P\sigma(SHW)=PF(H,A). Outputs reorder with nodes: equivariance. Permuting features without also permuting adjacency would describe a different graph and would not satisfy this calculation. 4 · Pool to get an invariant graph representation A sum readout is g=\mathbf1^\top H^{(L)} . Shared edge scoring and permutation-symmetric aggregation preserve analogous properties in message-passing models. 5 · Keep symmetry distinct from expressiveness A model can obey the correct permutation symmetry and still fail to distinguish particular graph structures or long-range relationships. Equivariance is a consistency property under relabeling, not a universal expressiveness guarantee. Depth brings both reach and bottlenecks After L local message-passing layers without extra long-range edges, information can travel at most L graph hops. Repeated propagation can suppress discriminative node directions: over-smoothing . In a connected undirected graph, pure row-normalized diffusion approaches a common stationary average, whereas symmetric normalization approaches a degree-weighted dominant subspace. Raw node values need not all become equal; the expandable calculation below makes the distinction explicit. Feature-variance loss under repeated graph diffusion. This isolates propagation; learned transformations, nonlinearities, and skip connections affect the behavior of a full GNN. Architectures · PDF p. 26 Over-squashing is different: information from a rapidly growing distant neighborhood must pass through narrow graph bottlenecks into a fixed-width vector. Representations can remain distinct while still failing to convey enough distant information. Distinguish homophily—connected nodes being similar—from heterophily, where neighboring nodes can differ systematically. Naive averaging can be inappropriate when the relation means opposition, complementarity, or a different role rather than similarity. Step by step Derive the degree-weighted diffusion limit behind oversmoothing Setting. Consider repeated linear propagation on a connected undirected nonnegative graph with self-loops: H^{(L)}=S^LH^{(0)} , where S=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2} . Assume the associated random walk is irreducible and aperiodic, so the eigenvalue one is simple and all other eigenvalues have absolute value below one. 1 · Find the leading eigenvector Let v=\tilde D^{1/2}\mathbf1 , whose entries are \sqrt{\tilde d_i} . Then Sv=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde D^{1/2}\mathbf1 =\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\mathbf1 =\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde D\mathbf1=v. Normalize it to u=v/\sqrt{\sum_i\tilde d_i} . 2 · Expand powers in an orthonormal eigenbasis Symmetry gives S=U\Lambda U^\top , with first column u and \lambda_1=1 . For one scalar feature, the limiting value at node i is h_i^{(\infty)}=\frac{\sqrt{\tilde d_i}}{\sum_j\tilde d_j} \sum_j\sqrt{\tilde d_j}\,h_j^{(0)}. The result lies in a one-dimensional node subspace. Nodes need not have identical raw values when their degrees differ. 4 · Compare row-normalized diffusion For R=\tilde D^{-1}\tilde A , the limiting rows are identical stationary-distribution averages: R^L\longrightarrow\mathbf1\pi^\top,\qquad \pi_i=\frac{\tilde d_i}{\sum_j\tilde d_j}. This is why “all nodes approach a common average” is literal for row-normalized connected aperiodic diffusion, but needs a degree-weighted qualification for symmetric normalization. 5 · Separate this mechanism from a full GNN theorem Learned transformations, nonlinearities, skip connections, disconnected components, and varying layer operators alter the dynamics. A raw feature-variance curve need not decrease monotonically under every such model. This simplified limit explains how repeated propagation can erase discriminative directions; over-squashing is a different limitation involving compression of many distant messages through narrow routes.
